items.title: Harold Danko interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 28, 2021
items.q: INTERVIEWER: ...you had Johnny Horton’s “The Battle of New Orleans,” and “Kansas City” by Wilbert Harrison. So my question is did a 12-year-old Harold Danko take note of any of this music...

ctx.x: Okay. So in 1959 there was actually a documentary called “The Year that Changed Jazz” and in that year you had the release of “Kind of Blue,” “Time Out,” Mingus “Ah Um,” “The Shape of Jazz to Come.” At the same time on the pop charts you had Johnny Horton’s “The Battle of New Orleans,” and “Kansas City” by Wilbert Harrison. So my question is did a 12-year-old Harold Danko take note of any of this music, and did it affect you in any particular way? If not, what did?

Well you know that’s about the year I really got interested in jazz and it was thanks to, I had two older brothers, both played saxophone, and so there was jazz in the house but they were much older than me and so they were not living at home, and I was the kid who they would come over and we would play some standard tunes or whatever. I didn’t know much. But then my brother got one of those big stereo things and played “Milestones” actually. And that did it for me. I heard “Milestones” on a stereo where there…
